transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-11-12
Start: 09:30 PT
Duration: ~40 minutes
Attendees: Sam (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Leo (Redwood DevOps); James, Priya, Carlos, Anita (Aurelia)

Summary: quick POC checkin to review week-2 throughput numbers, iterate batching params (continuous batching), set concurrency targets, and agree next runs. Slight transcription noise; some product names misrecognized.

Topics: perf numbers, batching, queueing/backpressure, SLA targets, next runs

Transcript:
[00:00] Sam Torres: hey everyone, thanks for joining — we'll do like 40 minutes today. quick agenda: run review, tuning knobs, decide next sustained run.
[00:16] James Lee: thanks. we saw an uptick in errors at about 20k tokens per minute, that coincided with a p99 jump. trying to understand whether it's batching or our front-end concurrency.
[00:30] Maya Patel: ok great. quick context: on Redwood side we ran three modes — baseline (no batching), continuous batching with batch_size target 8, and aggressive batch pooling with target 16. each run was 30 minutes and we measured tokens/sec, p50/p95/p99 latencies, and GPU util.
[00:48] Priya Singh: when you say continuous batching, is that the prefix cache-enabled flow? we've seen cache thrash with variable prompts.
[01:02] Maya Patel: good question. for these runs we used KV cache enabled and prefix caching on repeated user sessions. there was some thrash in the mid-run when sequence lengths spiked, which affected the batching efficiency.
[01:18] Carlos Mendez: quick clarif — our expected traffic shape is 120 RPS at peak but with bursts to 300 RPS for short windows. our p99 SLA target is 450 ms for user-facing endpoints.
[01:36] Sam Torres: noted. so today we'll focus on throughput and tail latencies; next call we can do reliability/failover.
[01:44] [02:05] Maya Patel: ok run-by-run numbers — baseline (no batching): tokens/sec ~3.2k, p95 380ms, p99 720ms, GPU util 46%. continuous-batch target=8: tokens/sec ~6.8k, p95 420ms, p99 810ms, GPU util 71%. aggressive batch target=16: tokens/sec ~9.3k, p95 540ms, p99 1.1s, GPU util 89%.
[02:40] James Lee: so bigger batches increased throughput but hurt p99 — expected. can you explain the concurrency impact?
[02:52] Leo Chen: from infra side, when we raised concurrency (parallel inflight requests) we saw queueing at the batcher — the runtime has a per-worker queue and a global queue; if concurrency is high you end up with larger batch aggregation but also higher head-of-line blocking when a long sequence blocks a batch.
[03:20] Maya Patel: yes exactly. the important knobs are: max_concurrency (how many requests a worker will process concurrently), batch_latency_target (how long to wait to form a batch), and queue_size_limits. we tested max_concurrency 8, 16, 24 in runs. with concurrency=24 and batch_target 25ms we got best sustained tokens/sec but the p99 increased due to a small number of long sequences.
[03:55] Anita Rao: is there a way to prioritize short requests? many of our user flows are short confirmations vs long document summarizations.
[04:08] Maya Patel: you can do multi-queue with priority tagging — short requests routed to a low-latency queue that uses smaller batch targets and preemptive scheduling. Redwood supports weighted queueing policies; we can show a config.
[04:30] James Lee: cool. please show the config and what tradeoffs look like.
[04:36] Sam Torres: we attached a sample yaml in the drive; Maya, can you summarize the config now?
[04:44] Maya Patel: sure — main pieces: queue_policy: {priority_queues: [short, normal], weights: [0.7, 0.3]}; short_queue: batch_target=10ms, max_batch=8; normal_queue: batch_target=30ms, max_batch=24; worker_concurrency=24; global_queue_limit=100. note: transcription may bungled the braces — the uploaded file has canonical format.
[05:12] Priya Singh: what about backpressure? if short queue saturates, will normal queue steal capacity?
[05:21] Leo Chen: by default we allow borrowing — when short queue empty its slots can be used by normal queue, but with priority tokens preserved. there is also a hard_global_limit to prevent OOM and GPU thrash.
[05:36] Carlos Mendez: we saw a case where a single long request blocked others and caused p99 spikes — is there a way to cap per-request token processing or preempt long runs?
[05:50] Maya Patel: preemption is tricky at model runtime level; we prefer two strategies: 1) request splitting (chunk long texts) or 2) soft timeouts + fallback model (lower-cost shorter-response model) via routing. Redwood supports automatic fallback routing to a lower-latency variant when queue_delay exceeds threshold.
[06:12] James Lee: fallback routing sounds promising. will fallback change semantics for us? our product requires consistent hallucination characteristics.
[06:22] Maya Patel: fallback models can be pinned to variants with similar temp/decoding configs to minimize regression; we also have evaluation hooks to compare outputs against golden prompts so you can detect regression.
[06:34] [06:55] Sam Torres: question for Aurelia: what's the acceptable p99 for backend-heavy endpoints vs user interactive?
[07:02] Priya Singh: interactive <450ms, backend async jobs can be up to 2s. most user-facing calls are interactive.
[07:15] Maya Patel: ok that clarifies — we'll aim for a config that prioritizes short interactive requests.
[07:22] James Lee: on the dedicated pool — any tips on GPU packing? we're using A100s with 80GB but our model is a 30B parameter variant.
[07:34] Leo Chen: quantization and kernel selection matter; the runtime chooses kernels based on sequence len. we saw a 12-18% throughput gain by using int8 quant + packing two workers per GPU for that model size, but it increases variance.
[07:52] Maya Patel: also consider pinned batch sizes on dedicated nodes to avoid fragmentation. continuous batching helps on shared pools but dedicated can be tuned to fixed bins for predictable latency.
[08:05] Carlos Mendez: for the sustained run you propose, what metrics will you share? we want raw traces and the batch-level logs.
[08:13] Maya Patel: we'll share per-request latency histograms, batch composition logs (sizes, sequence_len distribution), GPU util, and queue length over time. also include token counts and error rates.
[08:27] James Lee: perfect. any gotchas with KV cache and concurrency?
[08:34] Maya Patel: yes — high concurrency with KV cache and variable prefixes can increase cache misses and cause work duplication; we suggested session-affinity routing where repeat sessions go to same worker to maximize KV hits. that reduces GPU work and improves p99.
[08:52] Priya Singh: is session-affinity compatible with autoscaling?
[08:58] Leo Chen: yes, but there is a tradeoff: affinity pins load and can make autoscaling less nimble. we recommend a hybrid: short-lived affinity windows (e.g., 10 minutes) combined with cache warming during scale events.
[09:12] [09:40] Sam Torres: ok wrap-up: immediate plan is a 2h sustained run on dedicated pool with concurrency=24, priority queues enabled with short_queue batch_target=10ms, normal_queue 30ms; we'll include session-affinity and fallback routing. Redwood to upload logs and config.
[09:58] James Lee: sounds good. one last question — how would this work with our SSO and audit logging requirements?
[10:06] Sam Torres: no issues — private deployments include SAML SSO, KMS integrations, and audit logs. for pilot we're on hosted but can mirror logs into your SIEM; we'll send the security sheet.
[10:18] Anita Rao: thanks, appreciate quick turnaround.
[10:22] Maya Patel: thanks everyone. we'll post the run results and follow up with a proposed on-site demo week after.
[10:30] End of call
